newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Dhaka, Delhi agree to combat insurgency.
newsitem.headline: Dhaka, Delhi agree to combat insurgency.

text.p: Bangladesh and India have agreed to cooperate in combating insurgencies in their border regions, Bangladesh's senior foreign ministry official said on Monday.

"It (insurgency) has been a serious problem at both sides of the border for quite sometime. We had positive discussions on the issue," Farooq Sobhan told reporters after official talks between Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and the visiting Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday.
Sobhan said both sides agreed to reactivate a joint working group to investigate insurgencies.
He said the group comprising senior officials of the interior and foreign ministries would meet soon.
India has faced insurgency problems in its northeastern states bordering Bangladesh, Burma and China.
Tribal insurgents in Bangladesh have been fighting a bush war since 1973 for autonomy of the 5,500 sq mile (14,200 sq-km) Chittagong Hill Tracts bordering India and Burma.
Fights between security forces and tribal Shanti Bahini insugents have so far claimed 8,500 lives in the Hill Tracts and forced more than 50,000 tribespeople to take refuge in northeast India.
Gowda arrived on Monday on a two-day visit to Bangladesh, less than a month after the two countries signed a historic water-sharing accord that ended a decades-old dispute.
He was accompanied by a 17-member entourage, which includes External Affairs Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, Home Minister Indrajit Gupta and Foreign Secretary Salman Haider.

Officials in Dhaka described the visit as a landmark. The said it would help cement relations after Hasina and Deve Gowda signed a 30-year treaty in New Delhi last December on sharing water from the Ganges River, which flows through India and Bangladesh.
The treaty ended a dispute which had been simmering since 1974, when India built a barrage on the Ganges to hold back water near its border with Bangladesh.

Officials said the prime ministers would discuss the repatriation of Bangladeshi tribal refugees from India, trade and increasing cooperation among member-states of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC), which also comprises Pakistan, Sri Lanka, Bhutan, Nepal and the Maldives.
"The visit is a goodwill one but repatriation of the Chakma refugees, trade and SAARC matters will feature prominently in talks between the two premiers," an official told Reuters.
An official in Deve Gowda's office in New Delhi earlier said: "The prime minister is not going to Dhaka with a bag of demands or concessions."
India helped Bangladesh win a 1971 independence war against Pakistan, but ties between Dhaka and New Delhi since have been often soured by distrust and fear.
Relations started improving after Hasina, daughter of Bangladesh's slain independence leader Sheikh Mujibur Rahman, came to power following a general election last June.
The water accord put a "seal of trust" on warming ties, officials say.

A widening trade gap in favour of India remains a major Bangladeshi concern. In 1995/96 (July-June), Bangladesh imported goods worth $1.1 billion from India but its exports were a paltry $70 million, officials said.
